analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to post pay ranges for job openings and share them with applicants and employees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee until the Congress ended, with only 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to make it illegal for employers to post a job without a pay range, to withhold a pay range from an applicant before discussing pay, or to withhold an employee's own pay range at hire and annually after. It also barred employers from retaliating against workers who invoked these rights, and set penalties: up to $10,000 in civil fines, plus $1,000–$10,000 in damages per affected worker or actual damages, with attorneys' fees and class actions allowed. The bill never moved after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Job applicants and current employees, who would learn the expected pay range before negotiating, for their own job and equivalent positions. Workers in lower-paying fields and those who under-negotiate tend to gain the most from posted pay ranges, since pay secrecy has historically let employers pay similar workers different amounts for the same work.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a wage or wage range in every public or internal job posting, so applicants see the pay before applying rather than after months of interviews.
Requires employers to tell an applicant the pay range before discussing compensation, and to tell each employee their own range at hire, at least annually, and on request.
Makes it illegal to refuse to interview, hire, or promote someone for exercising these rights, so workers can ask about pay without fearing retaliation.

Gives workers a way to enforce the rule themselves: statutory damages of $1,000–$10,000 per violation (or actual damages, whichever is greater), attorneys' fees, and the ability to sue on behalf of similarly situated coworkers, on top of civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation for the employer.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would bear the cost of building pay scales for every position, adding ranges to all postings, and answering annual employee requests — plus fines, damages, and legal fees when they fail. Some of that cost could be passed on in prices, and some employers would face upward pressure on wages where posted ranges revealed below-market pay.

drawbacks.text: Compliance is a real cost, especially for small businesses without HR departments: the bill requires a pay range for every posting, disclosures at hire and annually, and creates fine and lawsuit exposure for mistakes.

The 'wage range' is whatever the employer anticipates 'in good faith,' so an employer could post a very wide range and stay technically compliant while still telling applicants little; the bill sets no limit on how broad a range can be.

The statutory damages of $1,000–$10,000 per violation plus class actions could generate significant litigation over technical paperwork errors rather than actual pay harm, and employers would face this under both federal and any stricter state or local transparency laws at once.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is real but moderate: posted pay ranges improve bargaining, yet the bill's good-faith definition allows wide ranges that dilute the effect. The costs fall on employers in compliance and litigation exposure, and the damages structure invites disputes over paperwork. States like Colorado and New York have adopted similar posting requirements, so employers would not have been facing an unprecedented demand. On balance a modest, enforceable win for workers, though a version with tighter range definitions and scaled penalties for small employers would have been better designed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never held a hearing or a vote, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the Salary Transparency Act on March 14, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
Only 2 House members cosponsored the bill, both Democrats, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever taken on it.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and any bill not passed by then dies; the complete action list for this bill ends with the committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers keep the status quo: no federal requirement to post pay ranges, and pay remains negotiable in private. Workers gain nothing from this bill.

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Sponsor; non-voting delegate for the District of Columbia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 2 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no roll-call split exists; the only support in the record came from the Democratic sponsor and 2 Democratic cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled House committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Pay secrecy lets employers learn each candidate's salary history and previous pay while the candidate cannot see what others earn, which tends to hold down offers. A posted-range mandate narrows that information advantage, which is why employer groups generally oppose federal transparency requirements.

industries.industry: HR software and payroll compliance vendors
industries.note: A federal pay-range mandate would create demand for tools that maintain pay scales and audit postings, so compliance vendors would profit from the same rule that helps workers see pay.
